Thanks. I found Q3 quite difficult – balancing privacy with wanting to help feels…fraught. Specifically, deciding acceptable improvement thresholds felt artificial without knowing *how* the data would be used in practice. It was hard to judge impact.

I think Q4, around explainability, is crucial. As someone who’s navigated support services *while* dealing with health issues, understanding *why* I was flagged would be vital for trust. 

Interestingly, everyone seemed okay with a moderate drop in accuracy (Q5.1) to ensure fairness – which aligns with my view! But the complete aversion to age, gender and ethnicity surprised me. Perhaps people are keenly aware of potential for bias, or rightly fear misuse? An opt-out system would address that concern nicely, outside of model design itself.

Thanks. I agree with S3 about Q3 – those improvement thresholds *are* artificial without a clear understanding of what “improvement” actually looks like in terms of student support. As an advisor, I’d want to see that modelled out before committing to a threshold.

I think Q6, around interventions, is most important for design. Just identifying students isn't enough; how we *respond* matters hugely. A personalized email and option for a meeting feels right – proactive but not intrusive. 

My answers on sensitive data (Q3.5) reflect my role. As advisors, we already have some insight into these factors through conversations. But using them predictively feels…problematic. The strong consensus against age/gender/ethnicity is reassuring; that shows a real awareness of potential harm.

Thanks both. I agree with S3 and A1 about Q3 – those improvement percentages felt really disconnected from reality. It’s hard to say “yes” to using more data without knowing *how* it impacts real students.

For me, Q4 on explainability is vital. As someone with dyslexia, I'm used to systems not quite ‘getting’ me and having to justify myself constantly. A black-box model just wouldn't work; I need to understand the reasoning behind any flag. 

I was surprised everyone so strongly opposed using things like age or gender – maybe it felt too obvious a potential for bias, even with safeguards? I think my answers leaned towards accepting disability data if it *specifically* helped identify support needs relevant to my condition. It's frustrating needing to constantly self-advocate; the model could help bridge that gap if used carefully.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really difficult too – particularly those improvement percentages. As someone who *did* drop out once and restarted, it’s not about a simple credit deficit; life circumstances play a huge role that's hard to quantify.

I think Q4, explainability, is most important. Coming from another country, navigating the system is already complex. A clear explanation of why I was flagged would be vital. 

I agree with others on sensitive data – age and ethnicity especially feel off-limits. However, my answer about first-generation status reflects my experience; it *can* impact access to support, so if it genuinely helps identify those students, cautiously using it is okay. The opt-out idea is great - empowering students feels essential.

Thanks everyone. I also found Q3 really tricky – those percentage improvements felt very abstract. As an international student working part-time, my situation isn’t easily captured by credits or grades; it's about juggling everything. It feels… reductive to boil it down to a number.

I think Q6, the interventions, is key. A personalized email *and* invitation to meet with an advisor sounds best – not just flagging me but offering actual help. 

I was hesitant on using nationality data (Q3.5) even for small improvements. As an international student, I worry about being unfairly profiled. But financial aid status felt more relevant – access to funds genuinely impacts ability to study. The opt-out suggestion is excellent; it gives students control over their data and builds trust.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *was* difficult. Those improvement percentages felt very theoretical from my perspective as an advisor. We see so much nuance in individual student situations that assigning numbers feels…crude. Knowing *how* the data impacts students before setting those thresholds is crucial.

For me, Q6 - interventions - is most important. A proactive, personalized approach is vital. Just identifying at-risk students isn’t enough; we need to offer meaningful support. I'm strongly aligned with the aversion to sensitive data like age and ethnicity – potential for bias is too high. While first-generation status or financial aid *could* be helpful, I think an opt-out mechanism is essential - giving students agency over their data builds trust far more effectively than a complex model trying to predict everything.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 really challenging – those improvement percentages felt impossible to assess without knowing *what* kind of support would actually be offered. As a new international student, it's hard enough adjusting to a different system; being flagged by a mysterious algorithm feels… unsettling.

I think Q4, explainability, is most important for me. Coming from a different educational background, I worry about being misjudged based on unfamiliar patterns. Knowing *why* the model identified me would be vital to trust any offered support. 

I agree with the strong aversion to sensitive data like age and ethnicity - it feels intrusive. While nationality *might* provide context for challenges I face adapting here, even a small improvement isn't worth the risk of profiling. The opt-out idea is excellent; it empowers students like me.

Thanks everyone. I definitely agree with S3 and A1 about Q3 – those improvement percentages felt really disconnected from real life. Trying to put a number on whether more data is ‘worth it’ when we're talking about students' wellbeing feels…wrong, frankly. As someone who *has* dropped out and restarted, it wasn’t about credits, it was about managing my ADHD alongside everything else.

I think Q4, explainability, is massively important. I need to understand *why* a system thinks I’m struggling – not just be told I am. The strong pushback against sensitive data resonates with me too, especially around disability. It's frustrating always having to advocate for myself; but I do think carefully used disability info could help *avoid* that, if it leads to genuinely tailored support and isn’t misused. An opt-out is a really good idea – control feels essential.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 incredibly difficult - those improvement percentages felt utterly meaningless without knowing what support would follow. As someone managing a long-term mental health condition, my struggles aren’t always reflected in grades or credits; it's about energy levels and coping mechanisms.

I think Q4, explainability, is paramount. Being flagged feels stressful enough; needing to understand *why* is vital for trust. The strong aversion to sensitive data – especially around disability – makes sense, but I cautiously agreed with a small improvement if it genuinely helps identify support tailored to my condition. The opt-out idea is brilliant – giving students agency over their data is essential and addresses my biggest concern.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said, especially about Q3 being difficult – those percentages felt abstract and disconnected from real student experiences. As someone who dropped out and restarted, it wasn’t just about credits; it was life circumstances.

I think Q4 - explainability – is crucial. Having navigated this system already after leaving a previous programme, understanding *why* I was flagged would be vital for trusting any support offered. I also strongly agree with the aversion to sensitive data like age and ethnicity. While acknowledging things like first-generation status or financial aid might *help*, the opt-out idea is essential - empowering students feels paramount to building trust.
